page.mentor_intro: Antibody-drug conjugates have reset the ceiling for HER2-positive breast cancer. Trastuzumab deruxtecan — a HER2 antibody carrying a topoisomerase-I payload with a high drug-to-antibody ratio — succeeded where earlier ADCs stalled and now defines later-line, and increasingly earlier, treatment of advanced disease. Managing ADCs well means mastering their distinctive toxicities (notably interstitial lung disease) and understanding how they fit into the wider HER2 landscape of monoclonal antibodies, tyrosine-kinase inhibitors and dual blockade.

teaching_points.claim: Trastuzumab deruxtecan is an antibody-drug conjugate consisting of a humanised anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody linked to a topoisomerase-I inhibitor payload (DXd), with a high drug-to-antibody ratio.

T-DXd was evaluated in patients with HER2-positive unresectable/metastatic breast cancer in the phase II DESTINY-Breast01 trial, and practical guidance addresses optimising its management in clinical practice.
Single-arm meta-analysis of T-DXd in HER2-expressing solid tumours confirms its efficacy and safety profile across tumour types.

HER2-positive breast cancer carries five-year survival around 30% at the advanced stage, and anti-HER2 treatment development — now including ADCs — has produced a paradigm shift in management and outcomes.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of ADCs versus TKIs and dual blockade, and re-challenge strategies after progression, are not settled.
Interstitial lung disease monitoring and management protocols vary, and long-term safety data continue to mature.
mcq_angles: ADC structure and mechanism (antibody, linker, payload, drug-to-antibody ratio).
DESTINY-trial lineage and where T-DXd sits in the treatment sequence.
T-DXd adverse effects: interstitial lung disease, nausea, myelosuppression.
ADC versus TKI versus dual blockade selection in advanced HER2-positive disease.
case_hooks: A patient progresses on trastuzumab-pertuzumab and T-DM1; plan the ADC next step and its monitoring.
A patient on T-DXd develops a dry cough and ground-glass change on CT; recognise and manage ILD.
page.gaps: Regimen sequencing tables, ILD grading-management algorithms, and biosimilar/earlier-line trial results (DESTINY-Breast03/04 details) are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against current guidelines before approval.

page.mentor_intro: A handful of polyposis syndromes explain a small but preventable fraction of colorectal cancer, and they reward precise recognition: FAP and its attenuated form, MUTYH-associated polyposis, the hamartomatous syndromes (juvenile polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers), and the Lynch syndromes nearby. Genetic testing costs have collapsed but referral of high-risk patients lags — so the clinical skill is suspecting the syndrome from polyp burden, age and family history, then channelling the patient into surveillance or risk-reducing surgery that genuinely prevents cancer.

teaching_points.claim: Hereditary adenomatous polyposis syndromes, including FAP and rarer variants, increase lifetime risk of colorectal and other cancers; updated European guidelines (38 experts) standardise their clinical management.

Inherited cancer syndromes are responsible for approximately 3-5% of all colorectal cancers, and although genetic-testing costs have plummeted, awareness and referral of high-risk patients remain the rate-limiting step.
Around 10% to 16% of colorectal cancer patients carry a pathogenic variant in a cancer-susceptibility gene, spanning a broader hereditary-colorectal-cancer syndrome landscape than polyposis alone.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome is a rare autosomal-dominant precancerous condition conferring increased gastrointestinal cancer risk, and should be suspected when hamartomatous polyposis features cluster in a family.

uncertainties: Optimal surveillance intervals and the threshold for prophylactic colectomy vary by syndrome, age and genotype, and are individualised in guideline practice.
Chemoprevention (NSAIDs in FAP) modifies polyp burden but its effect on cancer endpoints is not definitive.
mcq_angles: FAP: hundreds of adenomas, APC gene, prophylactic colectomy, upper-GI surveillance.
MUTYH-associated polyposis: autosomal recessive, attenuated phenotype.
Hamartomatous syndromes: juvenile polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers (STK11) and their extracolonic cancers.
When to refer for genetic testing: Amsterdam/Bethesda-style criteria and polyp-count thresholds.
case_hooks: A 28-year-old has hundreds of colonic adenomas and a family history of early colon cancer; outline FAP management.
A teenager with mucocutaneous pigmentation and small-bowel hamartomas; identify the syndrome and its surveillance needs.
page.gaps: Peutz-Jeghers and serrated-polyposis specifics, desmoid-disease management in FAP, and surveillance interval tables are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the full European polyposis guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in northern European populations and one of the most satisfying to treat: the biochemical signature is elevated transferrin saturation, the gene is usually HFE C282Y, and venesection removes the excess iron before it destroys organs. The tragedy is underdiagnosis — arthropathy, diabetes, cirrhosis and cardiomyopathy are preventable when phlebotomy starts early, which is why unexplained fatigue with abnormal iron studies should always prompt the ferritin-and-transferrin-saturation pair.

teaching_points.claim: Haemochromatosis is characterised by elevated transferrin saturation and progressive iron loading that mainly affects the liver; early diagnosis and treatment by phlebotomy can prevent cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, arthropathy and other complications.

Hereditary haemochromatosis is one of the most common genetic disorders among persons of northern European descent, with recent advances in diagnosis, management and molecular diagnostic testing reflected in the ACG guideline.
Haemochromatosis is overdiagnosed in patients without true iron overload and underdiagnosed in many patients; early diagnosis by genetic testing and therapy are emphasised.
Most patients remain asymptomatic, but others develop advanced organ damage — arthropathy, diabetes — that reduces quality of life and survival, defining the treatment urgency.

Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder that disrupts iron homeostasis, causing systemic iron overload, and is the most common inherited disorder among people of northern European ancestry.

uncertainties: Penetrance of HFE C282Y homozygosity is incomplete — many carriers never develop iron overload, complicating screening policy.
The role of hepcidin-pathway agents for patients unable to tolerate phlebotomy is investigational.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic sequence: transferrin saturation and ferritin first, HFE genotyping to confirm.
Phlebotomy targets and maintenance regimens.
Organ complications to screen for at diagnosis (liver, glucose, joints, heart, skin).
Incomplete penetrance and who actually needs treatment.
case_hooks: A 48-year-old man with fatigue, arthralgia and transferrin saturation 78% is found to be C282Y homozygous; plan management.
A patient's ferritin is very high but transferrin saturation is normal; decide whether this is haemochromatosis.
page.gaps: Transferrin-saturation/ferritin thresholds, phlebotomy dosing schedules, and non-HFE genotype management are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the EASL 2022/ACG 2019 full guidelines before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Roughly a third of phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry an identifiable germline mutation, and the genotype now organises everything: VHL, NF1, RET, and the SDHx genes each carry distinct tumour spectra, malignancy risk and surveillance rhythms. A young patient, a family history, or a paraganglioma rather than adrenal tumour should all trigger genetic testing — not as an academic exercise but because it changes who gets screened, for what, and how often.

teaching_points.claim: Pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas have a distinctive molecular landscape allowing assignment to clusters by genetic alteration; around 30-35% of Caucasian patients harbour germline mutations, underpinning personalised management.

Phaeochromocytomas are rare adrenal-medulla tumours that may be sporadic or part of a hereditary syndrome, and a considerable number carry germline or somatic mutations inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 is a complex autosomal-dominant disorder caused by germline NF1 tumour-suppressor mutations, with characteristic pigmentary features and a well-recognised phaeochromocytoma association.

Plasma or fractionated urine metanephrines are the biochemical test of choice for diagnosis, and the preoperative approach to phaeochromocytoma centres on alpha-blockade before any surgical manipulation.

uncertainties: Surveillance intervals and imaging modalities differ by genotype and are individualised rather than uniform.
SDH-mutation risk stratification, including for phenocopies such as SDHA and the paediatric surveillance question, is evolving.
mcq_angles: Genotype-phenotype map: VHL (renal, pancreatic, CNS haemangioblastoma), NF1 (cafe-au-lait, neurofibromas), SDHx (paraganglioma-dominant, GIST, pituitary).
When to suspect and test for germline disease: young age, family history, multifocal or extra-adrenal disease.
Biochemical diagnosis: plasma-free or urinary fractionated metanephrines.
Preoperative management: alpha-blockade before beta-blockade, volume repletion.
case_hooks: A 29-year-old with a paraganglioma and a family history of renal tumours; choose the genetic work-up and surveillance plan.
A patient with phaeochromocytoma needs adrenalectomy; sequence the preoperative medical management.
page.gaps: Gene-specific surveillance protocols (VHL, SDHx imaging schedules), malignancy-risk estimates by mutation, and RET/MEN2 linkage are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against Endocrine Society guideline before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Hereditary spherocytosis and elliptocytosis are disorders of the red-cell skeleton: defects in spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 or protein 4.2 weaken the membrane, splenic conditioning does the rest, and the result is a chronic haemolysis that announces itself through jaundice, gallstones and a positive family history. The laboratory signature is the spherocyte (or elliptocyte) on the film, and modern diagnosis mixes EMA-binding and osmotic-fragility studies with genetic testing.

teaching_points.claim: Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis and stomatocytosis are inherited disorders caused by defects in various red-cell membrane proteins; the ICSH guideline standardises their laboratory diagnosis given heterogeneous clinical, biochemical and genetic presentations.

Membrane structural defects lead to hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis, producing haemolysis; significant advances in diagnosis and clinical management of these inherited membrane disorders have been made.

Hereditary erythrocyte membrane disorders are caused by mutations in genes encoding transmembrane or cytoskeletal proteins, with decreased cell deformability and shortened erythrocyte survival as the main consequences.
Structural understanding of inherited red-cell membrane disorders explains altered cell function, reduced red-cell survival and the resulting haemolytic anaemia.

uncertainties: Thresholds for splenectomy — balancing haemolysis control against infection and thrombotic risk — are individualised and not standardised in the retained sources.
Genotype-phenotype correlation remains imperfect, complicating prognostication from molecular results alone.
mcq_angles: Spherocytes on film: HS versus warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (DAT differentiates).
Diagnostic tests: EMA binding, osmotic fragility, ektacytometry, genetics.
Complications: gallstones, aplastic crises (parvovirus B19), splenomegaly.
Elliptocytosis spectrum and hereditary pyropoikilocytosis.
case_hooks: A teenager with intermittent jaundice, gallstones at 19 and a positive family history; work through diagnosis.
A patient with spherocytes and a negative DAT has a sibling needing assessment; outline family screening.
page.gaps: Splenectomy indications and vaccination/management around it, EMA-binding protocol detail, and genotype-specific counselling are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the ICSH guideline full text before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Herpes simplex encephalitis is the neurological emergency where the treatment decision precedes the diagnosis: acyclovir must start on suspicion, because delay measurably worsens outcome and no surrogate marker can safely exclude HSE early. HSV-1 is the commonest sporadic encephalitis in adults, PCR of CSF is the diagnostic mainstay, and the modern complication to recognise is autoimmune encephalitis that can follow the infection — so deterioration after apparently successful treatment is not necessarily failure.

teaching_points.claim: Advances in antiviral medications and supportive treatments have equipped physicians to combat the most severe manifestations of HSV disease; prompt recognition and treatment of HSV-1 encephalitis are essential.

Encephalitis is most commonly caused by viral infection, especially HSV type 1, although autoimmune causes such as NMDA-receptor-antibody encephalitis are increasingly recognised — a differential that shapes empirical therapy.
Herpes simplex encephalitis has been successfully treated with acyclovir, though it remains a cause of significant morbidity even with treatment.

uncertainties: Optimal acyclovir duration and whether oral follow-on therapy adds benefit are not resolved in the retained abstracts.
The frequency and management of post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis (NMDAR-antibody) is increasingly recognised but not quantified in the retained sources.
mcq_angles: Empirical acyclovir on suspicion — treat before PCR confirmation.

page.mentor_intro: Most skin infections presenting in primary care are three diagnoses wearing different disguises: impetigo (honey-crusted, staphylococcal or streptococcal), herpes simplex (grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, recurring at the same site) and tinea (annular, scaly, advancing edge). The craft is pattern recognition plus judicious treatment — topical agents for localised disease, systemic agents when infection is extensive or deep, and a low threshold for reconsidering the diagnosis when a 'common infection' fails to respond.

teaching_points.claim: Common cutaneous infections of bacterial, viral and fungal origin are frequently encountered by clinicians in all fields, and an evidence-based review highlights treatment options and management across these classes.
Skin and soft-tissue infections in primary care range from uncomplicated impetigo to potentially lethal necrotising fasciitis, requiring careful severity triage.
Common cutaneous viral infections in children include warts, molluscum contagiosum, hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpes simplex.

uncertainties: Antibiotic choice and duration for impetigo vary by local resistance patterns, which the retained sources do not address.
When (and whether) antiviral therapy for recurrent mucocutaneous HSV changes natural history is not resolved in the retained abstracts.

HSV versus zoster versus impetigo pattern recognition.

page.mentor_intro: Shingles is the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus from a sensory ganglion, and it earns its place in the curriculum through two facts: it is common (about a million US cases a year, lifetime risk around 30%) and it hurts twice — acutely, and as post-herpetic neuralgia that can persist for months. Antivirals work best within 72 hours, ophthalmic and disseminated disease are emergencies, and recombinant vaccination has changed the prevention equation for older adults.

teaching_points.claim: Herpes zoster is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus within sensory ganglia, classically a painful unilateral vesicular eruption, with post-herpetic neuralgia among its principal complications.
There are an estimated 1 million cases of herpes zoster annually in the United States with an individual lifetime risk of 30%, and cell-mediated immunity decline drives reactivation.
Herpes zoster is a major health burden seen most commonly in those aged 50 and over, in immunocompromised patients and in those on immunosuppressant drugs.
In older adults, zoster presents as a unilateral self-limited dermatomal rash, but postherpetic neuralgia is a common and often dominant sequela.

uncertainties: Optimal management of established post-herpetic neuralgia remains difficult, with mixed evidence across drug classes.
Vaccination policy details (age thresholds, recombinant vs live attenuated) vary by country and are not settled in the retained sources.
mcq_angles: Dermatomal distribution: which levels, and why ophthalmicus (V1) is an emergency.
Antiviral window: treat within 72 hours, and later if new lesions appear.
Post-herpetic neuralgia risk factors and management options.
Recombinant zoster vaccine: who, when, and why it outperforms live vaccine.
case_hooks: A 72-year-old has a painful T8 dermatomal eruption that began yesterday; prescribe and counsel.

page.gaps: Antiviral agent selection/dosing, corticosteroid role, and PHN treatment algorithms are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against infectious-diseases/pain guidance before approval.

page.mentor_intro: A hiatal hernia is the stomach's migration through the diaphragmatic hiatus — the sliding type I being by far the commonest and mostly an incidental partner of reflux, while the para-oesophageal types (II-IV) carry mechanical complications like volvulus, obstruction and bleeding. Most need no treatment; the ones that do are either reflux-dominant (managed as GERD, with the ASGE guideline framing diagnosis and therapy) or mechanical (where surgical repair becomes the conversation).

teaching_points.claim: Esophageal hiatal hernia involves abnormal entry of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity and is classified by the relationship of the oesophagogastric junction to the diaphragm; the sliding type I is the most frequent category.
GERD pathogenesis is complex, involving reflux exposure, epithelial resistance and visceral sensitivity, and hiatal hernia is a key anatomical amplifier of reflux.
The ASGE 2025 guideline provides an evidence-based approach to diagnosing and managing GERD — the framework within which reflux symptoms attributed to hiatal hernia are managed.

uncertainties: Which sliding hiatal hernias benefit from surgical fundoplication beyond reflux control is individualised and debated.
Surveillance intervals for para-oesophageal hernias managed non-operatively are not standardised in the retained sources.
mcq_angles: Type I (sliding) versus types II-IV (para-oesophageal) hernias and their complications.
Hiatal hernia as a reflux amplifier: the anatomical rationale.
When an incidental hernia needs no treatment at all.
Red flags of mechanical complications: volvulus, obstruction, bleeding, anaemia.
case_hooks: An incidental sliding hiatal hernia is found on a chest X-ray; decide what (if anything) to do.
An elderly patient with a large para-oesophageal hernia develops post-prandial pain and retching; recognise the emergency.
page.gaps: Surgical indications and techniques (fundoplication, mesh), Cameron-lesion management, and giant-hernia work-up are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against surgical/ASGE guidance before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic, painful, under-recognised disease of the pilosebaceous unit in intertriginous skin — nodules, abscesses and draining tunnels in the axillae, groin and inframammary folds, with a prevalence around 1% and a heavy quality-of-life burden. Assessment uses severity staging (Hurley), and treatment escalates from topical and systemic antibiotics through biologics (anti-TNF) to surgery for tunnelling disease — a sequence the European S2k guideline formalises.

teaching_points.claim: The European S2k guideline (updated from the 2015 S1) provides a decision aid for selecting, implementing and assessing appropriate therapy for hidradenitis suppurativa.
HS is a chronic inflammatory disease characterised by painful deep-seated nodules, abscesses and draining tunnels in the axillary, inguinal, genitoanal or inframammary areas.
HS is a chronic, debilitating inflammatory disease derived from the pilosebaceous unit affecting approximately 1% of the general population, with nodules, abscesses and tunnels as clinical hallmarks.
HS is a complex immune-mediated disorder initially presenting as folliculitis that can progress to advanced lesions such as fistulas requiring extensive surgical intervention.

uncertainties: Optimal sequencing of biologics and the role of surgery early versus late in tunnelling disease remain practice-dependent.
Disease-modifying therapy that prevents progression, rather than suppressing flares, is not yet established.
mcq_angles: Hurley staging (I nodules/abscesses, II sinus tracts/scarring, III diffuse involvement).
Treatment ladder: topical clindamycin -> tetracyclines -> anti-TNF biologics -> surgery.
Comorbidity associations: obesity, smoking, metabolic syndrome, depression.
Differentiating HS from boils and Crohn's-related perianal disease.
case_hooks: A 26-year-old with recurrent axillary abscesses and scarring is told she has recurrent boils; recognise HS and stage it.
A patient with Hurley II disease fails antibiotic therapy; discuss biologic options using the guideline framework.
page.gaps: Hurley-staging definitions, specific antibiotic/biologic regimens and dosing, and surgical technique selection are not covered by the retained abstracts; verify against the S2k full guideline before approval.
